questions.lo: Chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
questions.q: In every chemical reaction, what happens to the atoms?
options: Some of them are used up and then destroyed
They are rearranged into new substances
Some change into atoms of other elements
They stay in the same molecules as before
questions.explain: Yes. The atoms separate from the atoms they were joined to and join up in new ways, making new substances. No atom is made, destroyed or changed.
optionWhy: You may have thought atoms get used up because reactants seem to disappear. In fact every atom is still there after the reaction, joined in a new substance.
Yes. The atoms separate from the atoms they were joined to and join up in new ways, making new substances. No atom is made, destroyed or changed.
You may have thought a reaction turns one kind of atom into another. In fact atoms never change in a chemical reaction; only the way they are joined changes.
You may have thought the molecules just mix or stick together. In fact the atoms come apart and join up differently, so new molecules form.

questions.lo: Chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
questions.q: The diagram shows hydrogen reacting with chlorine. Which statement about the reaction is correct?
options: The same atoms are joined in a new way
The atoms have changed into new atoms
Some of the atoms have been used up
The two molecules have just mixed
questions.explain: Yes. Count them: 2 hydrogen and 2 chlorine atoms before, and 2 of each after. The atoms have separated and joined up differently, making hydrogen chloride.
optionWhy: Yes. Count them: 2 hydrogen and 2 chlorine atoms before, and 2 of each after. The atoms have separated and joined up differently, making hydrogen chloride.
You may have thought a reaction turns atoms into new kinds of atom. In fact the diagram shows the same hydrogen and chlorine atoms after the reaction, joined in a new way.
You may have thought atoms are used up in a reaction. In fact there are 2 hydrogen and 2 chlorine atoms both before and after; none has gone.
You may have thought the molecules stay whole and simply mix. In fact the H₂ and Cl₂ molecules have come apart, and new HCl molecules have formed.

questions.lo: Chemical reactions as the rearrangement of atoms
questions.q: Which of these changes is a chemical reaction?
options: Chocolate melting in the sun
Sugar dissolving in hot tea
Mixing two paints to make green
Wood burning on a bonfire
questions.explain: Yes. Burning wood makes new substances, such as carbon dioxide, water and ash, that were not there before. It cannot be reversed.
optionWhy: You may have thought melting makes a new substance because the chocolate looks different. In fact melting is a change of state: the chocolate sets again when it cools.
You may have thought the sugar turns into something new because it disappears. In fact the sugar is still there, spread out in the tea, and evaporating the water would leave it.
You may have thought a colour change always means a reaction. In fact the blue and yellow paint particles are just mixed; no new substance forms.
Yes. Burning wood makes new substances, such as carbon dioxide, water and ash, that were not there before. It cannot be reversed.

questions.lo: Representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
questions.q: Iron reacts with sulfur to make a single product. Which word equation is correct?
options: iron + sulfur → iron sulfate
iron + sulfur → iron sulfide
iron sulfide → iron + sulfur
iron + sulfur = iron sulfide
questions.explain: Yes. Iron and sulfur join to make iron sulfide. The reactants go on the left, the product on the right, and the arrow means 'reacts to make'.
optionWhy: You may have mixed up -ide and -ate. A sulfate also contains oxygen, but only iron and sulfur reacted, so the product is iron sulfide.
Yes. Iron and sulfur join to make iron sulfide. The reactants go on the left, the product on the right, and the arrow means 'reacts to make'.
You may have put the product on the left. Reactants go on the left of the arrow and products on the right; iron and sulfur are what you start with.
You may have thought the arrow means 'equals'. In fact it means 'reacts to make': iron sulfide is a new substance, not the same as iron and sulfur.

questions.lo: Representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
questions.q: Magnesium (Mg) burns in oxygen (O₂) to make magnesium oxide (MgO). Which symbol equation is balanced and correct?
options: 2Mg + O₂ → Mg₂O₂
Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
Mg + O₂ → MgO + O
questions.explain: Yes. Left: 2 Mg and 2 O. Right: 2MgO has 2 Mg and 2 O. The formulae are unchanged and every atom balances.
optionWhy: You may have changed the small numbers to make it balance. The formula of magnesium oxide is MgO and must not change; balance with big numbers in front instead.
You may have balanced the oxygen and stopped. Check every atom: the right now has 2 Mg but the left has 1, so you also need 2Mg.
Yes. Left: 2 Mg and 2 O. Right: 2MgO has 2 Mg and 2 O. The formulae are unchanged and every atom balances.
You may have written the spare oxygen atom as a product. A lone oxygen atom is not made; 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO puts both oxygen atoms into magnesium oxide.

questions.lo: Representing chemical reactions using formulae and using equations
questions.q: How many oxygen atoms are on each side of this equation? CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
options: Left 2, right 3
Left 4, right 3
Left 4, right 2
Left 4, right 4
questions.explain: Yes. 2O₂ has 2 × 2 = 4 oxygen atoms. On the right, CO₂ has 2 and 2H₂O has 2 × 1 = 2, so 4 in total.
optionWhy: You may have ignored the big numbers. 2O₂ means two O₂ molecules (4 O), and 2H₂O means two water molecules (2 O), so it is 4 on each side.
You may have doubled only the first symbol in 2H₂O. The big 2 doubles the whole molecule, so 2H₂O has 2 oxygen atoms and the right has 2 + 2 = 4.
You may have counted the O in H₂O as no atoms because it has no small number. It stands for one atom, so 2H₂O has 2 oxygen atoms and the right has 4.
Yes. 2O₂ has 2 × 2 = 4 oxygen atoms. On the right, CO₂ has 2 and 2H₂O has 2 × 1 = 2, so 4 in total.

questions.lo: Combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
questions.q: Magnesium burns in air with a bright white flame. Which substance is made?
options: Soot made of carbon
Carbon dioxide and water
Nothing: it burns away
Solid magnesium oxide
questions.explain: Yes. A metal burns by joining with oxygen to make its oxide: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, a white powder.
optionWhy: You may have thought burning always leaves soot. Soot is carbon, and magnesium contains no carbon, so the product is magnesium oxide, a white powder.
You may have used the equation for burning fuels. Carbon dioxide and water need carbon and hydrogen, which magnesium does not contain; it makes magnesium oxide.
You may have thought the magnesium is destroyed as it burns. In fact its atoms join with oxygen to make magnesium oxide, which weighs more than the magnesium did.
Yes. A metal burns by joining with oxygen to make its oxide: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide, a white powder.

questions.lo: Combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
questions.q: Calcium carbonate is heated strongly. What does it form?
options: Calcium, carbon and oxygen gas
Water and carbon dioxide gas
Calcium oxide and carbon dioxide
Only melted calcium carbonate
questions.explain: Yes. This is thermal decomposition: calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide. Many metal carbonates break down like this to a metal oxide and carbon dioxide.
optionWhy: You may have thought decomposition splits a compound into its elements. In fact it gives simpler compounds: calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
You may have used the equation for burning a fuel. Calcium carbonate contains no hydrogen, so no water can form; it gives calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
Yes. This is thermal decomposition: calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide. Many metal carbonates break down like this to a metal oxide and carbon dioxide.
You may have thought heating only melts a solid. In fact strong heating breaks calcium carbonate down into new substances.

questions.lo: Combustion, thermal decomposition, oxidation and displacement reactions
questions.q: Copper is heated in a hot, blue Bunsen flame. Its surface turns black. What is the black layer?
options: Copper oxide, as oxygen joined the copper
Soot (carbon) left on it by the flame
Copper changed by heat, with nothing added
Copper that has turned into carbon
questions.explain: Yes. Copper reacts with oxygen from the air to make black copper oxide. Gaining oxygen like this is oxidation.
optionWhy: Yes. Copper reacts with oxygen from the air to make black copper oxide. Gaining oxygen like this is oxidation.
You may have thought heating in a flame always leaves soot. A hot, blue flame does not make soot; the black layer is copper oxide.
You may have thought heat alone changed the copper. In fact oxygen from the air joined on, making a new substance, copper oxide.
You may have thought one element can turn into another. Copper atoms cannot become carbon atoms; the copper has joined with oxygen.

questions.lo: Defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
questions.q: Which statement is true of every acid?
options: It eats away any material it touches
It can be neutralised by an alkali
It has the same pH as all other acids
It bubbles and fizzes on its own
questions.explain: Yes. Every acid reacts with an alkali and is neutralised, making a salt and water. That is how acids and alkalis are defined.
optionWhy: You may have thought every acid burns and eats things away. Many acids, such as citric acid in lemons, do not; what every acid does is react with an alkali.
Yes. Every acid reacts with an alkali and is neutralised, making a salt and water. That is how acids and alkalis are defined.
You may have thought pH only shows acid or alkali. In fact acids have different pH values, from 0 up to just below 7.
You may have thought fizzing is part of being an acid. An acid on its own does not fizz; bubbles appear only when it reacts with something.

questions.lo: Defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
questions.q: A substance dissolves in water. Which result shows that the substance is an alkali?
options: It neutralises acids
It turns blue litmus red
It has a pH below 7
It reacts with nothing
questions.explain: Yes. A substance that dissolves in water and neutralises acids is a base that dissolves: an alkali. Its solution also has a pH above 7.
optionWhy: Yes. A substance that dissolves in water and neutralises acids is a base that dissolves: an alkali. Its solution also has a pH above 7.
You may have mixed up the litmus colours. Turning blue litmus red shows an acid; an alkali turns red litmus blue.
You may have thought the pH scale runs the other way. Below 7 is acidic; an alkali has a pH above 7.
You may have thought alkalis are harmless and do nothing. In fact alkalis react with acids, and can damage skin and eyes.

questions.lo: Defining acids and alkalis in terms of neutralisation reactions
questions.q: When an alkali neutralises an acid, what happens to the acid?
options: It breaks down on its own and stops being acid
It reacts with the alkali to make a salt
It is simply stopped from burning anything
It is only diluted by the water in the alkali
questions.explain: Yes. Neutralisation is a reaction between the acid and the alkali. It makes a salt and water.
optionWhy: You may have thought neutralisation is the acid breaking down. In fact the acid reacts with the alkali; both are used up and a salt and water form.
Yes. Neutralisation is a reaction between the acid and the alkali. It makes a salt and water.
You may have thought an alkali only stops the acid working. In fact the alkali reacts with the acid; it is not a shield.
You may have thought the alkali just waters the acid down. Diluting does not neutralise an acid; the alkali reacts with it.

questions.lo: The pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
questions.q: Which statement about the pH scale is correct?
options: Higher numbers are more acidic
Neutral solutions have a pH of 0
Lower numbers are more acidic
All acids have exactly the same pH
questions.explain: Yes. The lower the pH below 7, the more acidic the solution. pH 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline.
optionWhy: You may have thought a bigger number means more acid. In fact higher numbers are more alkaline; pH 1 is far more acidic than pH 5.
You may have thought 'no acid' belongs at zero. Neutral is pH 7, in the middle; pH 0 is extremely acidic.
Yes. The lower the pH below 7, the more acidic the solution. pH 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline.
You may have thought pH only tells you acid or alkali. Acids have different pH values: the lower the number, the more acidic.

questions.lo: The pH scale for measuring acidity/alkalinity; and indicators
questions.q: Blue litmus paper is dipped into a solution and stays blue. What does this show?
options: It is not acidic, as an acid turns it red
It is alkaline, as blue means alkali
It is acidic, as acids turn litmus blue
It is neutral, as nothing changed
questions.explain: Yes. Acids turn blue litmus red. Blue litmus stays blue in both neutral and alkaline solutions, so you only know the solution is not acidic.
optionWhy: Yes. Acids turn blue litmus red. Blue litmus stays blue in both neutral and alkaline solutions, so you only know the solution is not acidic.
You may have thought blue litmus staying blue proves an alkali. Blue litmus was blue to start with, and stays blue in neutral solutions too.
You may have swapped the litmus colours. Litmus is red in acids, so an acid would have turned the blue paper red.
You may have thought no colour change means neutral. Blue litmus also stays blue in an alkali, so the solution could be neutral or alkaline.

questions.lo: Reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
questions.q: Zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid. One product is zinc chloride. What is the other product?
options: Water, which stays in the beaker
Hydrogen gas, which fizzes off
Oxygen gas, which fizzes off
Zinc oxide, a white solid
questions.explain: Yes. metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. The salt here is zinc chloride, and the bubbles of gas are hydrogen.
optionWhy: You may have mixed this up with neutralisation. Acid + alkali gives a salt and water, but metal + acid gives a salt and hydrogen.
Yes. metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. The salt here is zinc chloride, and the bubbles of gas are hydrogen.
You may have thought the bubbles are oxygen. A metal and an acid make hydrogen, which burns with a squeaky pop.
You may have thought a metal always makes its oxide. No oxygen gas is used here; the zinc ends up in the salt, and the other product is hydrogen.

questions.lo: Reactions of acids with metals to produce a salt plus hydrogen
questions.q: Magnesium is added to hydrochloric acid and it fizzes. Which test shows that the gas is hydrogen?
options: A lit splint gives a squeaky pop
A glowing splint bursts into flame
It turns clear limewater milky
It turns damp blue litmus red
questions.explain: Yes. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lit splint is held at the mouth of the tube.
optionWhy: Yes. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lit splint is held at the mouth of the tube.
You may have thought the gas is oxygen. A glowing splint relighting is the test for oxygen; metal + acid makes hydrogen.
You may have thought any fizzing gas is carbon dioxide. There is no carbon in magnesium or hydrochloric acid, so the gas is hydrogen.
You may have thought the gas is acidic because it comes from the acid. In fact hydrogen is not an acid and does not turn litmus red; the test for it is a lit splint.

questions.lo: Reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
questions.q: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution, an alkali. What are the products?
options: Sodium chloride and water
Sodium chloride and hydrogen
Only the acid, now diluted
Nothing, as they cancel out
questions.explain: Yes. acid + alkali → salt + water. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, so the salt is sodium chloride.
optionWhy: Yes. acid + alkali → salt + water. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, so the salt is sodium chloride.
You may have mixed this up with acid + metal. An acid and an alkali make a salt and water, not hydrogen.
You may have thought the alkali just waters the acid down. In fact the acid reacts with the alkali, making sodium chloride and water.
You may have thought the acid and alkali cancel each other out to nothing. In fact their atoms make new substances: sodium chloride and water.

questions.lo: Reactions of acids with alkalis to produce a salt plus water
questions.q: The graph shows the pH as an alkali is slowly added to an acid. Which statement is correct when 20 cm³ of alkali has been added?
options: No acid has reacted, as the pH is not 7
It is more acidic than it was at the start
Some acid and alkali have turned into nothing
Some of the acid has been neutralised
questions.explain: Yes. Each drop of alkali reacts with some acid, so the pH has risen from 1 to about 2. It reaches 7 only when all the acid has reacted.
optionWhy: You may have thought neutralisation only happens at pH 7. In fact the alkali reacts as soon as it is added; the pH reaches 7 only when all the acid is used up.
You may have thought a higher pH means more acidic. The pH has risen from 1 to about 2, so the mixture is less acidic than at the start.
You may have thought the acid and alkali cancel out to nothing. In fact their atoms are still there, in the salt and water made.
Yes. Each drop of alkali reacts with some acid, so the pH has risen from 1 to about 2. It reaches 7 only when all the acid has reacted.

figure.alt: A line graph. The horizontal axis is labelled volume of alkali added (cm³), with marks at 0, 10, 20 and 30. The vertical axis is labelled pH, with marks at 0, 7 and 14, and a dashed line across at pH 7. The line starts at pH 1 at 0 cm³ and rises slowly to about pH 2 at 20 cm³. Near 25 cm³ it rises very steeply through pH 7, then levels off at about pH 12 by 30 cm³.

questions.lo: What catalysts do
questions.q: Manganese(IV) oxide speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen. Afterwards, any solid left is filtered off and dried, with none spilled. How does its mass compare with the start?
options: It is the same as at the start
It is less, as some was used up
It is zero, as it became the oxygen
It is more, as it took in oxygen
questions.explain: Yes. Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst: it speeds up the reaction but is not used up, so the same mass is recovered.
optionWhy: Yes. Manganese(IV) oxide is a catalyst: it speeds up the reaction but is not used up, so the same mass is recovered.
You may have thought a catalyst is used up. In fact all of it is recovered unchanged at the end.
You may have thought the oxygen comes from the catalyst. The oxygen comes from the hydrogen peroxide; the manganese(IV) oxide is all still there.
You may have thought the catalyst joins with the products. In fact it is left over unchanged, so its mass is the same.

questions.lo: What catalysts do
questions.q: The graph shows the volume of gas made by the same reaction with and without a catalyst. What did the catalyst change?
options: The total volume of gas made
Only how fast the gas was made
Which gas the reaction made
Whether any gas was made at all
questions.explain: Yes. Both lines level off at 50 cm³, so the same amount of gas was made; the catalyst only made it faster.
optionWhy: You may have thought a catalyst gives more product. Both lines end at 50 cm³, so the total is the same.
Yes. Both lines level off at 50 cm³, so the same amount of gas was made; the catalyst only made it faster.
You may have thought a catalyst changes the products. It speeds up the same reaction, which makes the same gas.
You may have thought the reaction needs the catalyst to happen. The dashed line shows gas being made without it, only more slowly.

figure.alt: A line graph. The horizontal axis is labelled time (s), with marks at 0, 100 and 200. The vertical axis is labelled volume of gas (cm³), with marks at 0, 25 and 50. A solid line labelled with catalyst rises steeply and levels off at 50 cm³ after about 60 s. A dashed line labelled without catalyst rises more slowly and levels off at the same height, 50 cm³, after about 150 s.
